checks.claim: Key: a force is a push or a pull
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a force is a push or pull upon an object resulting from the object's interaction with another object'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A burst of energy' (force is not energy)
checks.note: RESPeCT: 'Students often confuse force with energy'; a force 'describes an interaction between two objects', while energy is what is conserved and transferred. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A kind of motion'
checks.note: A force can cause an object to 'accelerate, decelerate, or change direction'; it changes motion, it is not motion. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A kind of matter'
checks.note: A force is an interaction (a vector quantity with magnitude and direction), not a substance. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the wind pushes the ball; the fence pushes back to stop it (a still object exerts a force)
checks.note: RESPeCT lists 'inanimate or inert objects don't exert force' as a misconception, with the example of a wall stopping a thrown ball.

checks.claim: Grade note: Florida SC.5.P.13.1 names pushes and pulls; TEKS 5.7A
checks.note: SC.5.P.13.1, grade 5: 'Identify familiar forces that cause objects to move, such as pushes or pulls, including gravity acting on falling objects.' TEKS 112.7 (Grade 5, adopted 2021) 7(A) confirmed at law.cornell.edu.

checks.claim: Key: the rope moves only when one team pulls harder (unbalanced forces)
checks.note: Net force zero gives 'no change in the object's velocity'; a nonzero net force produces acceleration whose size 'depends on the imbalance of forces'. Physics nuance, not an error: which team WINS is set by the grip of feet on the ground (Grokipedia Tug_of_war: traction 'through friction with the ground'), but for the rope itself to start moving, the pull on one end must exceed the other (by what the rope's small mass needs), so the key is literally true. Standard 5th-grade picture of balanced/unbalanced forces (Labster, Oxford Science 7, Teachoo all use it).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Both teams must pull harder than before'
checks.note: Equal harder pulls stay balanced; NGSS: 'balanced forces pushing on a box from both sides will not produce any motion at all'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Both teams must keep pulling for longer'
checks.note: Zero net force for any length of time leaves velocity unchanged. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Gravity must stop holding the rope down'
checks.note: Gravity acts downward and does not oppose sideways motion; the horizontal pulls decide. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: balanced pulls leave the rope unchanged however hard or long; unbalanced move it toward the stronger side
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'balanced forces result in no net change in motion'; 'unbalanced forces produce acceleration proportional to the net force'.

checks.claim: Grade note: TEKS 5.7A equal and unequal forces
checks.note: 19 TAC 112.7 Grade 5 (adopted 2021), 7(A): 'investigate and explain how equal and unequal forces acting on an object cause patterns of motion and transfer of energy'.

checks.claim: Key: a rock dropped from a tall ladder speeds up all the way down
checks.note: Terminal velocity is 'asymptotically reached, not instantaneously'; even a 5 mm hailstone has about 14 m/s and a baseball about 33 m/s (HyperPhysics, https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/airfri2.html); Grokipedia gives hailstones 20-50 m/s. A rock dropped about 5-10 m reaches only about 10-14 m/s in about 1-1.4 s, so it is still speeding up when it lands. Key true.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It speeds up, then holds steady' (could air resistance make this true?)
checks.note: Only after a long fall: a skydiver reaches about 53 m/s after about 12 s. A dense rock from a ladder never gets near its terminal speed. Truly wrong for this rock (it would be right for a feather or leaf, which is why the stem's 'rock' matters).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It falls at one steady speed' and 'It starts fast, then slows down'
checks.note: A dropped object starts from rest and accelerates at about 9.8 m/s^2. Both truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: 'near the ground a falling thing gains almost 10 metres per second of speed every second'
checks.note: True for a rock (g = 9.80665 m/s^2, 'almost 10' is fine), but stated of 'a falling thing' it is false for light things a child knows: Grokipedia gives falling leaves a terminal speed of about 0.5-2 m/s and snowflakes under 1 m/s, so they never gain anything like 10 m/s each second. Fix: say 'a dropped rock' instead of 'a falling thing'.

checks.claim: Context: 'Only a very long fall, far longer than this one, ever stops speeding up.'
checks.note: As a general claim this is false: a thin flat plate 'reaches it quickly', and leaves, paper and feathers stop speeding up within moments of being dropped. It is true only of a dense thing like the rock. Fix the context's last two sentences to: 'Gravity's pull on the falling rock is unbalanced (the air pushes back on a rock only a little), and an unbalanced force keeps changing an object's speed: near the ground a dropped rock gains almost 10 metres per second of speed every second. A rock stops speeding up only after a very long fall, far longer than this one; light things such as leaves and feathers stop much sooner, because the air holds them back.'

checks.claim: Context: 'Gravity is an unbalanced force on the falling rock'
checks.note: Loose but acceptable at grade 5: air drag also acts, but gravity far exceeds it on a rock, so the net force is unbalanced. The suggested fix above words it more exactly.

checks.claim: Grade note: Florida SC.5.P.13.1 names gravity acting on falling objects; TEKS 5.7A
checks.note: Verified: 'including gravity acting on falling objects' (grade 5).

checks.claim: Key: friction pushing against its motion slows and stops the kicked ball
checks.note: RESPeCT: 'The grass the ball rolls over and the air it moves through both exert forces that push the ball in the opposite direction of the kick, causing the ball to slow down and eventually stop.' Grokipedia Friction: friction acts 'always in the direction opposite to the impending or actual motion'; drag through air is 'fluid friction'; Grokipedia Rolling_resistance lists rolling friction among the friction types. Calling it friction is true at grade 5.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The force of his kick running out'
checks.note: RESPeCT: 'Objects don't contain force, so they can't run out of force.' Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Gravity pulling it back to a stop'
checks.note: On a flat field gravity pulls toward Earth's centre (down), not back against the roll. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Moving things stopping on their own'
checks.note: RESPeCT misconception 3, 'All objects slow down and eventually stop': 'If no forces are acting on a moving object, its motion will never change or stop.' Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: grass and air both push against the motion; a kick ends when the foot leaves; no store of force
checks.note: Matches RESPeCT. 'That rubbing force, friction' covering the air too is fine: Grokipedia Friction calls drag 'fluid friction'.

checks.claim: Grade note: TeachEngineering grades 3-5 ramp activity; Oak National Academy Year 5 friction lesson
checks.note: Oak page is titled 'Friction: plan KS2 | Y5 Science' and says 'Friction always acts in the opposite direction to the movement of an object.' TeachEngineering cub_measurement_lesson01_activity2 is Grades 3-5. (The other TeachEngineering friction lesson in facts.md, duk_friction_smary_less, is Grades 6-8, not 3-5; it is not cited in this grade note.)

checks.claim: Key: the car rolls a shorter way on shaggy carpet, which makes more friction
checks.note: TeachEngineering (Grades 3-5): cars 'roll best on smooth surfaces rather than the textured surfaces of carpets'; 'friction between the wheels and the ramp or floor slows it down'. Oak Y5 starter quiz: more friction on 'a rough surface'. (Physically much of a carpet's drag is rolling resistance from fibres giving under the wheels; Grokipedia Rolling_resistance lists rolling friction as a type of friction, so the key stays true.)

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Shorter on the wood, which makes more friction'
checks.note: 'There is usually less friction when two smooth surfaces slide past each other.' Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The same on both, since the ramp is the same'
checks.note: The floor's friction differs, so the rolls differ. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Longer on the carpet, which is soft and springy'
checks.note: Softness raises rolling resistance (energy lost to deformation; on compliant ground 'wheel sinkage dominates'); it does not lengthen the roll. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: friction is greater on rough surfaces; carpet fibres drag on the wheels; the ramp starts the car the same each time
checks.note: Grokipedia: roughness often increases 'the static friction threshold on rougher surfaces'; TeachEngineering: 'it is the roughness of the surfaces that determines the amount of friction'. Same car, same ramp, same release gives the same start.

checks.claim: Grade note: car on a ramp is the TEKS 5.7B investigation; TeachEngineering grades 3-5
checks.note: TEKS 112.7(7)(B), Grade 5: 'design a simple experimental investigation that tests the effect of force on an object in a system such as a car on a ramp or a balloon rocket on a string'. TeachEngineering activity confirmed Grades 3-5.

checks.claim: Key: to make a north-sliding puck swerve west, tap its east side (pushing it west)
checks.note: A nonzero net force 'produces linear acceleration in the direction of the net force'. A stick on the east side pushes west, so the puck gains a westward motion and veers west (north-west). Arbor Scientific's air-puck lab answer key: a single force perpendicular to motion gives 'direction changes' (https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0030/6207/1369/files/Air_Puck_lab1_answerkey.pdf). 'One tap' rules out hooking the puck and dragging it.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Its west side' (would push it east)
checks.note: A force has 'both magnitude and direction'; a push on the west side points east. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Its south side' (from behind speeds it up) and 'Its north side' (from in front slows it)
checks.note: Arbor Scientific answer key: a tap from behind in the direction of motion, 'Direction Same, speed increases'; a tap opposite the motion, 'Direction Same, speed decreases'. Both truly wrong, and the context's account of them matches.

checks.claim: Context: a push moves a thing the way the push points; east-side tap sends it west, west-side east, south speeds up, north slows
checks.note: NGSS PS2.A: 'Each force acts on one particular object and has both strength and a direction'; 'Forces that do not sum to zero can cause changes in the object's speed or direction of motion.' For a moving puck the push adds motion in its own direction, so 'the way the push points' is a fair grade-5 summary.

checks.claim: Grade note: NGSS PS2.A (strength and direction); TEKS 5.7A 'turning included'
checks.note: PS2.A quote verified (it is a grade 3 core idea, built on later, as the note says). TEKS 5.7A says 'patterns of motion'; 'turning included' is the writer's gloss, not TEKS wording, but not false.

checks.claim: Key: a pull toward Earth's centre keeps people all round the globe on it
checks.note: NGSS PS2.B: 'The gravitational force of Earth acting on an object near Earth's surface pulls that object toward the planet's center.' NASA Space Place: 'Gravity is the force by which a planet or other body draws objects toward its center'; 'Earth's gravity is what keeps you on the ground' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/what-is-gravity/en/).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The weight of the air above them'
checks.note: Air pressure comes from the weight of the air column but 'acts isotropically, equally in all directions', so it pushes up under a person as much as down on top; it holds no one on. Science Learning Hub names 'gravity exists due to the presence of air' as a misconception. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The pull of Earth's magnetism'
checks.note: Earth's field is only about 25-65 microtesla at the surface and people are not magnetic; gravity, not magnetism, holds them. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The push of Earth's spin'
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Rotation introduces a centrifugal effect that opposes gravity', so the spin slightly lessens the hold rather than giving it. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: down always means toward the centre, wherever a person stands; air, magnetism and spin do not hold anyone on
checks.note: 5-PS2-1 clarification: ''Down' is a local description of the direction that points toward the center of the spherical Earth.' (Earth's slight flattening and spin bend 'down' by a tiny fraction of a degree; irrelevant at this grade.)

checks.claim: Grade note: NGSS 5-PS2-1
checks.note: 'Support an argument that the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down.' Verified.

checks.claim: Key: gravity still pulls the resting book, just as hard as if it were falling
checks.note: Science Learning Hub, scientists' view: 'Gravity acts whether an object is moving or not.' The pull (the book's weight) is the same at rest or falling from that shelf.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'No, gravity stops once a thing is still'
checks.note: Listed misconception: students 'may think that gravity acts on an object while it is falling but then stops when it reaches the ground'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'No, the shelf blocks gravity's pull'
checks.note: The shelf does not block gravity; it pushes up and balances it: for a book at rest 'the net force is zero because supporting forces balance out'. Science Learning Hub: objects on a table or shelf stay put because of balanced forces. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Only a little, since it is not moving'
checks.note: Gravity's pull does not depend on motion. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: gravity pulls everything all the time; the shelf holds the book up
checks.note: RESPeCT: an object at rest has the downward force of gravity and 'the upward force of the surface the object is sitting on'.

checks.claim: Grade note: Science Learning Hub names 'gravity only acts on falling objects'
checks.note: Exact phrase verified on the page.

checks.claim: Key: the crate stays still because the floor pushes back on it just as hard (static friction balances the push)
checks.note: Grokipedia: static friction 'adjusts dynamically to match the applied tangential force', 'preventing motion as long as this force remains below the maximum threshold', and acts opposite to 'impending' motion. Florida SC.5.P.13.4 (grade 5): when a force is applied to an object 'but it does not move', an opposing force from the environment balances it. True at a 5th-grade level, and the context names the floor's push as friction.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The air around it holds it in place'
checks.note: RESPeCT lists the belief that 'air pressure, gravity, or an intervening object (like a table) keeps another object stationary' as a misconception; air pressure acts equally on all sides (Grokipedia Atmospheric_pressure). Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'His push is too weak to be a force'
checks.note: Any push is a force by definition; size does not decide that. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'No push can move a crate that heavy'
checks.note: Static friction has a maximum; a push above that threshold starts it sliding (a heavier crate only raises the threshold). Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: a push that moves nothing is still a force; friction pushes back just as hard; forces balanced; a harder push or friends would get it sliding
checks.note: Matches the static-friction threshold: once the push exceeds the maximum static friction the crate slides.

checks.claim: Grade note: Florida SC.5.P.13.4
checks.note: Benchmark SC.5.P.13.4, grade 5, verified: 'Investigate and explain that when a force is applied to an object but it does not move,' another opposing force from the environment balances it.

unit_notes: 8 ok, 1 error. The one error is in a context, not a key or choice: the falling-rock context (96060defa5) says 'a falling thing gains almost 10 m/s every second' and 'Only a very long fall ever stops speeding up', which are false for light things (leaves, feathers, snowflakes reach terminal speed almost at once); reword to be about the rock (fix given). Choice checks: the rock's 'speeds up, then holds steady' is truly wrong for a rock from a ladder (it lands at about 10-14 m/s, far below a dense rock's terminal speed of 30+ m/s); the crate key is correct static friction; the puck key (east side) is correct. Tug-of-war physics nuance noted (the winner is set by grip on the ground) but the key stays literally true for the rope. For the record: facts.md F7/F9/F10 lean on TeachEngineering duk_friction_smary_less, which is a Grades 6-8 lesson, not 3-5 (cub_measurement_lesson01_activity2 is the Grades 3-5 one); the friction facts themselves are confirmed by Grokipedia Friction and Oak's Year 5 lesson. No quotations or myths in the unit; no numbers that change over time.
